This study examines the combined impact of chord-to-radius ratio (c/R), blade camber, and preset pitch on cross-flow turbine performance.
The concepts of 'virtual camber' and 'virtual incidence' arise due to the curved trajectory of the blades in cross-flow turbines.
Net camber is defined as the sum of virtual camber and geometric camber, while net incidence is the sum of virtual incidence and preset pitch angle.
Positive net camber is expected to enhance lift production in the upstream portion of the turbine rotation, but decrease performance in the downstream region.
The experiments covered a range of c/R from 0.25 to 0.74 and optimal tip-speed ratios from 2.3 to 3.6.
Increasing toe-out preset pitch (more negative α_p) reduced performance in the upstream region but increased it downstream.
The optimal preset pitch at a given c/R or camber condition occurred at a relatively constant net incidence of 0° to +1°.
The experiments were conducted at diameter-based Reynolds numbers from approximately 1.6 × 10^5 to 2.7 × 10^5.
The authors noted that while Reynolds number and blockage were held constant, their influences could not be wholly removed and may have had secondary effects.
The study proposes using net camber and net incidence as composite variables to better understand turbine performance and design behavior.
Two experimental datasets were used in the analysis, one varying c/R, pitch, and blade count, and the other examining geometric blade camber and pitch.
The authors used the conformal transformation method of Migliore and Wolfe to calculate the virtual camber and incidence effects.
Positive virtual camber and incidence were found to enhance lift production in the upstream portion of the turbine rotation.
The authors hypothesized that the balance between upstream lift enhancement and downstream loss reduction determines the optimal turbine geometry.
The study suggests that c/R, camber, and pitch should be considered in conjunction to achieve an optimal turbine design.
